newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine police, jobless clash in Salta province.
newsitem.headline: Argentine police, jobless clash in Salta province.

text.p: Argentine police used rubber bullets, tear gas and water cannons on demonstrators blocking a road in Salta province on Friday in another violent episode among the recent wave of protests of unemployment.

Local media said nine people, including three women, were arrested. Television showed now familiar scenes of protesters, this time former state water company employees, burning tires on a highway and police trying to dislodge them.

"Our children are dying of hunger. We're not subversives, we just want the government to respond," shouted one of the protesters, along with slogans against President Carlos Menem and the International Monetary Fund.

The IMF has warned Menem of the dangers of ignoring such protests in a country with an unemployment rate of 17.3 percent. But Menem blames it all on "subversives" fomented by the political opposition ahead of October's mid-term elections in Congress.

Roadblocks have turned up in the southern province of Neuquen, in central Cordoba, Jujuy, Salta's neighbouring province, and other regions, but the worst violence was in Jujuy where 180 people were injured in three days of rioting.
The heavy-handed police reaction against shanty dwellers in Jujuy, where unemployment reaches 40 percent in some towns, was criticised by the Catholic church and the opposition.
But Interior Minister Carlos Corach said on Friday that the paramilitary border police involved "committed no excesses and no charges have been lodged against them."

After rebuking Catholic bishops for their criticism, and asking on Wednesday where people were dying of hunger in Argentina, Menem then urged his cabinet ministers and provincial governors on Thursday to "get back to your roots and try to make human development match our macroeconomic figures."

Since Menem came to power in 1989, Argentina has beaten hyperinflation down to zero and sustained healthy economic growth. But unemployment has nearly tripled, from just 6 percent in 1989 to over 17 percent by late 1996.
